newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian airline cargo up with shorter Asian route.
newsitem.headline: Canadian airline cargo up with shorter Asian route.

text.p: Canada's two major airlines say they expect to carry more cargo to Hong Kong by using new overfly rights obtained from China and Russia.

For Canadian Airlines International, which spearheaded negotiation for the rights, and Air Canada, the bilateral agreements will trim 45 minutes from the 13.5-hour trip from Vancouver to Hong Kong from October through April when aircraft have to buck strong Pacific headwinds.

"The distance is actually about the same, but by coming over Russia and China (rather than over Taiwan) we get out of those very strong headwinds sooner," said Capt Robert Weatherly, CAI's vice-president of flight operations.
The new westbound routing, which CAI inaugurates on Thursday, will mean a payload gain - more cargo, passengers or both - for a DC-10.
CAI operates a daily B-747-400 and adds two DC-10s a week during peaks like Christmas and Chinese New Year.
The 747s can reach Hong Kong now with a maximum payload, said Weatherly.

Air Canada, which flies Vancouver-Hong Kong four times a week, didn't negotiate the overfly rights but hopes to start using them by the end of October. It stands to reap a larger financial reward per flight.

For a B-747, the 45-minute reduction in flying time translates into a reduction in fuel load of 8.2 tonnes. Since Air Canada's B-747-400 combis are payload-restricted on the route, reducing fuel weight allows an equivalent increase in cargo payload.
Air Canada usually carries about 18-20 tonnes ex-Vancouver on aircraft designed to carry 39 tonnes.
With cargo rates at C$2.25/kilo, an eight-tonne cargo pickup will mean additional revenues of up to C$18,000 per flight for Air Canada, say industry officials.
Vancouver-Hong Kong "is a great market; any extra capacity we would sell 80-90 percent of the time," said Air Canada Cargo chief Robert Thomson.
Returning from Hong Kong, aircraft will stick to the old routing to gain maximum advantage of what become strong tail winds, said Weatherly.
To avoid overfly fees equivalent to about three-quarters of the fuel savings, CAI also will use the old air corridor from Vancouver during the summer months when headwinds are light, he said.
The rights apply purely to Hong Kong flights, but could serve as the basis for creating faster routings between the west coast of Canada and centres like Bangkok and Ho Chi Minh City, he said.
Cathay Pacific Airways also flies Vancouver-Hong Kong.

The British government has negotiated China overfly rights for Cathay, but vice-president Peter Langslow told Reuters that its B-747s already fly the route without payload restrictions. The savings of time and fuel would have to be weighed against the steep overfly fees.
More likely, Cathay first will use Chinese overfly rights on the longer Los Angeles-Hong Kong route, which is payload-restricted, said Langslow.
Cathay's ex-Vancouver freighter flights refuel in Anchorage in both directions, he added. -Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
